# Lints

The Gossamer linter ships 67 day-one checks. Each has a short
identifier suitable for `#[lint(allow(...))]` and a long-form
explanation available via `gos lint --explain <id>`. This page
is auto-generated from `gossamer-lint`; hand edits are
overwritten on the next run of `cargo xtask docs-lints`.

## `unused_variable`

Declares a `let` binding whose name is never read.
Prefix the name with `_` to silence explicitly (e.g. `_tmp`)
when the binding is intentional but unused.

## `unused_import`

A `use` declaration whose imported name is never referenced.
Remove the import or reference the name in the file.

## `unused_mut_variable`

A binding marked `mut` that is never reassigned. Drop the `mut`
keyword.

## `needless_return`

`return expr` at the tail of a block is the same as writing `expr`
by itself. Prefer the tail form for symmetry with the rest of
the expression language.

## `needless_bool`

`if cond { true } else { false }` is the same as `cond`. The
inverted form is `!cond`.

## `comparison_to_bool_literal`

`x == true` reads worse than `x`, and `x == false` reads worse
than `!x`. Drop the literal.

## `single_match`

A `match` with a single arm reads better as `if let PATTERN = ...`.
Single-arm `match` is almost always a half-written exhaustive match.

## `shadowed_binding`

A `let` binding shadows an earlier one: in the same block, or in a
nested block over a `let mut` of an enclosing one. The nested case
is usually an assignment written as a declaration: `let status =
"done"` inside an `if` leaves the outer `status` as it was. Assign
it with `status = ..`, or rename one of them to make the data flow
obvious.

## `unchecked_result`

`let _ = expr?` silently discards an error. Either handle the
`Err` branch explicitly or propagate with `?` so the caller sees it.

## `empty_block`

An empty `{}` block is almost always a mistake. Add an explicit
`()` tail if the block is intentional.

## `panic_in_main`

`panic!` inside `main` aborts without a clean exit code. Return a
`Result` from `main` and use `?` so the error propagates.

## `redundant_clone`

Calling `.clone()` on a literal or already-copied value is
redundant. Drop the call.

## `double_negation`

`!!x` collapses to `x` when `x: bool`. If the double negation is
intentional for truthiness coercion, use an explicit cast.

## `self_assignment`

Assigning a variable to itself does nothing. The statement is
usually the residue of a refactor - remove it.

## `todo_macro`

`todo()` and `unimplemented()` are placeholders, not shippable
expressions. Implement the branch before merging.

## `i64_only_container_family`

`std::collections::{queue,stack,deque,heap,ordered_*}` hold
`i64` only and return a new container from every mutator, which
duplicates `Queue`, `Stack`, `Deque`, `MinHeap`, `BTreeSet`, and
`BTreeMap` at a narrower element type.
Deliberately not auto-fixable: the two families differ in more
than spelling. `peek` answers `0` on an empty container where the
type answers `None`, so a mechanical rewrite would keep
type-checking and change what an empty container means.

## `no_effect_statement`

An expression statement that only computes - a path, a literal,
arithmetic over them - and hands its value to nothing.
A newline followed by `-`, `*`, or `&` starts a NEW statement, so
a continuation meant as part of the line above becomes one of
these. Join it to that line (end the previous line with the
operator, or parenthesise), or bind what it computes.
A builtin method that answers a new value and writes nothing -
`v.dedup()`, `s.trim()`, `s.to_uppercase()` - with its result
dropped is the error `GT0140`.

## `bool_literal_in_condition`

`if true { ... }` / `while false { ... }` - the branch is
decided at compile time. Drop the control-flow construct.

## `let_and_return`

`let x = expr; x` at the tail of a block is just `expr`. Drop
the needless binding.

## `collapsible_if`

`if a { if b { ... } }` can be combined into
`if a && b { ... }`. Easier to scan.

## `if_same_then_else`

Both branches of the `if` are identical. Drop the branch and
keep the body once.

## `needless_else_after_return`

`if cond { return X } else { Y }` - the `else` is unreachable
fall-through. Un-nest the `else` body.

## `self_compare`

Comparing a value to itself is always `true` (for `==`, `<=`,
`>=`) or `false` (for `!=`, `<`, `>`). Use the constant.

## `identity_op`

`x + 0`, `x - 0`, `x * 1`, `x / 1` all equal `x`. The operation
adds nothing but noise.

## `unit_let`

`let x = ()` binds the unit value, which is almost never useful.
Drop the `let`.

## `float_eq_zero`

Equality against a float literal its type cannot hold exactly,
such as `0.1` or `0.3`, with a value that is not computed in sight
(a parameter, a field). If that value comes from arithmetic, it
rounds to a neighbour of the decimal and the comparison is false.
Compare `(x - y).abs() < eps` with an explicit tolerance. A literal
the type holds exactly (`0.0`, `0.5`, `1.0`) is not flagged, and a
computed value against an inexact literal is the error `GT0142`.

## `empty_else`

`else {}` adds no information. Drop the else and let the `if`
stand alone.

## `match_bool`

`match b { true => ... false => ... }` is an `if` in disguise.
Rewrite as `if b { ... } else { ... }`.

## `needless_parens`

`(x)` without a trailing comma is a needless pair of parens -
`x` reads the same. `(x,)` is a one-tuple and means something
different. Closure parameters follow the same rule: write `|t|`,
not `|(t)|`.

## `manual_not_equal`

`!(a == b)` is just `a != b`. Prefer the direct operator.

## `nested_ternary_if`

Three or more `if / else if` layers that all test one value
against a pattern are a `match` written the long way. Rewrite
them as `match` on that value. A chain whose arms test
unrelated conditions, or compare with `<` and `>`, is left
alone: `match` would only move those into guards.

## `absurd_range`

A literal range whose lower bound exceeds its upper bound is
empty. Swap the bounds or double-check the intent.

## `string_literal_concat`

`"a" + "b"` can be written directly as `"ab"`. Let the
source reflect the final value.

## `chained_negation_literals`

`-(-x)` is `x`. The extra unary does nothing.

## `if_not_else`

`if !cond { A } else { B }` scans better as `if cond { B }
else { A }`. Flip the branches and drop the `!`.

## `empty_string_concat`

Concatenating an empty string literal is a no-op. Drop the
`"" +` or `+ ""`.

## `println_newline_only`

`println("")` already writes a newline. Don't pass `"\n"`
and don't call it twice to emit a blank line.

## `match_same_arms`

Two match arms share the same body. Either collapse them with
`|` alternation or extract the shared body into a helper.

## `manual_swap`

Three consecutive statements `let tmp = a; a = b; b = tmp` swap
two bindings via a temporary. Prefer a destructuring assignment
once the language supports it, or at minimum document why the
swap is needed.

## `consecutive_assignment`

Two back-to-back assignments to the same place - the earlier
value is dead before it's read. Drop the first or consolidate
the logic into one statement.

## `large_unreadable_literal`

Integer literals of five or more digits are easier to scan with
`_` as thousands separators: `1_000_000` instead of `1000000`.

## `redundant_closure`

`|x| f(x)` is a closure that just forwards to `f`. Pass `f`
directly.

## `empty_if_body`

An `if cond { } else { body }` is the same as `if !cond { body }`.
Invert the condition and drop the empty branch.

## `bool_to_int_match`

`match b { true => 1, false => 0 }` is an `if` in disguise that
happens to return an integer. Prefer `if b { 1 } else { 0 }`.

## `fn_returns_unit_explicit`

`fn f() -> () { ... }` is the same as `fn f() { ... }`. The
explicit `-> ()` is noise.

## `let_with_unit_type`

`let _: () = expr` annotates the binding with the unit type. If
`expr` was going to return `()` anyway, the annotation is noise.
If it wasn't, the annotation forces a coercion - use a plain
statement instead.

## `useless_default_only_match`

`match x { _ => expr }` always runs `expr` - the `match` adds
nothing. Drop the `match` (and add `let _ = x` if evaluating
the scrutinee has side effects).

## `unnecessary_parens_in_condition`

`if (cond) { ... }` wraps the condition in a single-tuple
expression. Drop the parens: `if cond { ... }`.

## `pattern_matching_unit`

`match () { ... }` has exactly one reachable arm. Drop the match
and run the body directly.

## `panic_without_message`

`panic()` with no argument leaves the post-mortem with nothing
to render. Always pass a brief explanation.

## `empty_loop`

`loop {}` with no body busy-waits forever at 100% CPU. Add a
`break`, a `continue`, or replace with a real wait primitive.

## `fill_loop`

A `for _ in 0..n { xs.push(value) }` loop that pushes the same
literal every iteration is the repeat literal spelled long:
`let xs = [value; n]` builds the identical vec in one expression
(byte-packed for `bool` / `u8` elements).

## `substring_byte_scan`

`s.substring(i, i + 1)` allocates a String per step of a scan.
`substring` takes byte offsets, so `s.byte_at(i)` reads the same
position directly as an `i64`: compare with byte literals
(`s.byte_at(i) >= b'0'`), do arithmetic on it
(`s.byte_at(i) - b'0'`), and render with `s.byte_at(i) as char`.
`s[i]` is not that byte: indexing counts Unicode scalars, so it
yields the `char` at character index `i`.

## `restated_field_default`

A struct literal writes a field with exactly the value the field
declares as its default (`result: 0` where the struct says
`result: u32 = 0`). A literal that leaves the field out takes the
default, so the written value says nothing; leave it out, and the
literal changes when the default does. `gos lint --fix` drops it.

## `redundant_default_derive`

`#[derive(Default)]` on a struct whose every field declares a
default. Such a struct already answers `T::default()` and `T {}`
from its own defaults, so the derive says nothing.
`gos lint --fix` drops `Default` from the derive.

## `non_camel_case_types`

A type, trait, enum variant, associated type, or type parameter
whose name is not `UpperCamelCase`, as Rust spells them: `Point`,
`HttpServer`, `KeyA`. A foreign type keeps its C spelling.

## `non_snake_case`

A function, method, parameter, local, field, or module whose name
is not `snake_case`, as Rust spells them. A single name in a pattern
matches a variant, struct, or const it names and binds otherwise, so
a binding written `Width` reads as a variant it is not. A foreign or
`#[export]` function and a `#[repr(C)]` struct's fields keep their C
spelling.

## `non_upper_case_globals`

A const or static whose name is not `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`, as Rust
spells them. A single name in a pattern matches the const it names,
so `limit =>` compares against a const `limit` rather than binding;
the upper case spelling keeps that visible. A foreign static keeps
its C spelling.

## `unjoined_task`

A task's handle bound by `let task = spawn(..)` and never used.
Nothing joins the task, so the program goes on without waiting for
it, and `main` can print, or return, before the task's work is done.
Call `task.join()` where that work must be finished, which also
answers the task's result. A task meant to run on its own is spawned
without a binding, `spawn(..)`; inside a `cohort { }` the cohort
joins every task when it ends.

## `lossy_cast`

An `as` conversion that can change the value: a narrowing integer
cast (`v as u8` with `v: i64`), a signed and unsigned swap, a cast
from a float to an integer, or between `char` and a type too narrow
for it. `as` keeps the low bits of an integer and saturates a float,
silently. Say which you mean: `v.try_into()` answers a `Result` that
is `Err` when the value does not fit, `(v & 0xFF) as u8` keeps the
low bits, `v.clamp(0, 255) as u8` saturates, and
`x.round().clamp(0.0, 255.0) as u8` rounds and saturates a float.
A cast the compiler can see fits (a literal in range, a widening
cast, a mask, a clamp to the target's range) is not reported.

## `closure_self_cycle`

A closure stored in a value it captures: `o.callback = Some(|| o.x)`,
or `handlers.push(|| handlers.len())`. A closure names the bindings it
captures, so the value holds the closure and the closure holds the
value. Neither is ever released, and the runtime does not collect the
cycle. Capture a weak reference instead: in `[weak o] || ..` the name
`o` is, inside the body, an `Option` that is `Some` while the value
lives and `None` once it is gone. `o.downgrade()` written before the
closure and upgraded inside it is the same capture.

## `signed_remainder`

A remainder compared with a positive number while the value divided
may be negative: `n % 2 == 1`. `%` answers a remainder with the sign
of the value it divides, as in C, Rust, and Go, so `-3 % 2` is `-1`
and the comparison is false for every negative odd `n`. Test
oddness with `n % 2 != 0`, or compare the remainder in `0..k` with
`n.rem_euclid(k) == r`, the same for every sign. A value shown to be
at least zero (an unsigned type, a mask, a literal `clamp`, `abs`,
`rem_euclid`, a `for` over a range from zero, an `enumerate` index)
is not reported.

## `split_shared_update`

A `sync::Shared` written with a value read from it under a separate
lock: `counter.set(counter.get() + 1)`. The `get` takes the lock and
releases it, and the `set` takes it again, so a write another
goroutine makes between the two is overwritten and lost.
`counter.update(|n| n + 1)` holds the lock across the read and the
write and stores what the callback answers.

## `day_duration`

A whole number of days, as a `Duration`, added to or taken from a
`time::Time`: `t + Duration::from_secs(86_400)`. A `Duration` is
elapsed time, so across a daylight-saving change the wall clock
moves by 23 or 25 hours and lands an hour off the time of day.
`t.add_date(0, 0, 1)?` moves the calendar date and keeps the time
of day.

## `unwrap_used`

Calling `.unwrap()` can panic when the value is `None` or `Err`.
Handle the missing value or error with `match`, `if let`, or `?`;
use `.unwrap_or(..)` when a fallback is appropriate. If a panic is
intentional, `.expect("reason")` gives it a useful message.

## `undeclared_return_value`

A signature with no return type answers a unit, so the value the
body's tail expression produces is discarded and the caller reads
the unit the signature promises. Return it with `-> T`, or write
`-> ()` to say the discard is deliberate.

## `option_rendered`

An `Option` is rendered with `{}` alongside other text, in an f-string
or a `println` / `format` template. When the value is `None`, the
output contains the word `None`; when it is present, it contains
`Some(..)`. An `Option` printed by itself, as in `println(opt)`, is
not flagged. Choose a user-facing value with `name.unwrap_or("guest")`,
`if let Some(n) = name`, or `match name`. Use `{name:?}` to show the
explicit `Some(...)` or `None` form.
